planting.note: Mount on a bark slab or moss pole, or grow loose in a hanging basket of chunky orchid mix; this miniature climbing epiphyte spreads by scrambling along its support rather than filling a pot.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light with no direct sun, which quickly scorches the thin foliage. Pearl laceleaf is a small, wiry-stemmed climbing epiphyte native from southern Mexico through the West Indies to Brazil, and it is happiest mounted on bark or moss, or planted in a shallow, fast-draining orchid-bark mix that mimics its life clinging to tree trunks in the wild. The narrow, glossy, lance-shaped leaves are only a few inches long but are produced in abundance along creeping stems, and mature plants reward growers with dangling spikes of small, pearly white to lilac berries that give the species its common name. Keep humidity high and the roots evenly moist but never soggy, letting the top of the mix dry briefly between waterings.

planting.note: Provide a sturdy moss pole or totem for climbing support and plenty of overhead room, since mature leaves are dramatically larger and more deeply divided than juvenile foliage.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with high humidity and warm, stable temperatures, since this hemiepiphytic rainforest species climbs into the canopy in its native Central and South American range and resents cold drafts or dry air. Foliage changes dramatically as the plant matures: young leaves are simple with just a few shallow lobes, while established specimens produce huge, deeply pedate leaves divided into a dozen or more finger-like segments, giving rise to the trade names Five Fingers and Fingers Anthurium. Use a chunky, well-aerated aroid mix that drains quickly, and water thoroughly when the top inch dries, since waterlogged roots invite rot in this otherwise vigorous grower. Give the plant a moss pole or similar support to climb as it matures, since larger leaf forms only develop once the plant is allowed to grow upward.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded greenhouse specimen in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; the upright rosette habit makes it a striking focal specimen rather than a trailing plant.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a coarse, fast-draining aroid mix; native to the rainforest understory of Venezuela and Colombia, Jenman's anthurium tolerates lower humidity and slightly cooler conditions better than many velvet-leaf collector species, making it a comparatively forgiving bird's-nest type for indoor growers. Thick, leathery, broadly elliptic leaves with undulating margins and prominent parallel veins emerge in a vase-shaped rosette, arching outward as the plant matures into a bold architectural specimen. Allow the mix to dry slightly between waterings rather than keeping it constantly moist, and feed lightly during the growing season, since this slower-growing species is more sensitive to fertilizer salt buildup than to underfeeding.
